Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix Terminal one-liner pulling ClickLock payload from compromised macOS host domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ClickLock LaunchAgent persistence (com.authirity.plist / com.chromer.plist) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ClickLock exfiltration/C2 to Telegram Bot API and GSocket relay from non-browser process · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] osascript fake macOS login-password dialog (ClickLock credential coercion) · [LLM] ClickLock coercion kill-loop terminating Finder/Dock/Activity Monitor at sub-second cadence
ClickFix Terminal one-liner pulling ClickLock payload from compromised macOS host domains AIDelivery High
Hunts the ClickLock initial-access step where a victim pastes an attacker-supplied Terminal command that curls/bashes a stealer payload from the compromised legitimate domains Group-IB attributed to the campaign. Article-specific because it pins on the four named hosting domains plus macOS shell download binaries. Rationale: Uses the four compromised hosting domains Group-IB named plus macOS download binaries; a shell process referencing these domains is high-fidelity delivery signal. Domains are single-source (Group-IB) so kept alongside behavioural anchors.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately cloning/curling from a domain that later gets flagged as compromised
  • Internal mirror of a package that happens to be hosted on one of these domains
  • Security researcher intentionally fetching the sample for analysis
  • Automation/CI runner on a macOS build agent fetching a dependency
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Terminal","iTerm2","osascript")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent — confirm parent is Terminal/iTerm and the URL path fetches a shell/zip payload rather than a legit asset. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the curl/bash chain, and block the four domains at proxy/DNS. Step 3 (hunt): On the same host look for follow-on osascript password dialogs, LaunchAgent writes (com.authirity.plist/com.chromer.plist), and outbound api.telegram.org connections.

| where FileName in~ ("curl","bash","sh","zsh","nohup")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("panalobet.ph","store.grafsynergy.com","cottonbox.co.il","gsnc.eu")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","bash","sh","zsh","nohup")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("panalobet.ph","store.grafsynergy.com","cottonbox.co.il","gsnc.eu")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

osascript fake macOS login-password dialog (ClickLock credential coercion) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ClickLock's core credential-theft primitive: osascript rendering a spoofed macOS password prompt (display dialog with a hidden-answer field) to capture the victim's system login password before Telegram exfiltration. Article-specific because Group-IB explicitly calls out osascript launching password dialogs as the detectable behaviour. Rationale: Pins on Group-IB's stated detection cue — osascript launching password dialogs — using the AppleScript 'display dialog' + 'hidden answer' construct that any credential-harvest prompt requires. Behavioural and self-contained, no IOC dependency.
ATT&CKT1056.002 T1059.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit admin tools (e.g. some VPN or backup installers) using osascript to prompt for a password
  • Corporate helpdesk scripts requesting sudo credentials via AppleScript
  • Homebrew/first-run apps requesting authorization through a dialog
  • Developer testing an AppleScript dialog
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Installer","softwareupdated","osascript_helper")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the dialog text and icon path in ProcessCommandLine — ClickLock spoofs the real username and a downloaded Apple icon; legit prompts name a specific app. Check the parent process (Terminal/unsigned binary = bad). Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, force-reset the user's macOS/login and directory password, revoke any SSO sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Look for a repeated killall loop of Finder/Dock, LaunchAgent persistence, and outbound Telegram API traffic on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "osascript"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "display dialog"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hidden answer","password")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "osascript"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "display dialog"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hidden answer","password")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

ClickLock coercion kill-loop terminating Finder/Dock/Activity Monitor at sub-second cadence AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ClickLock's forced-interaction loop that terminates key macOS apps (Finder, Dock, Terminal, Activity Monitor, Console, System Settings, Spotlight) every 200–210ms so only the password dialog remains on screen. Article-specific because it targets the exact app set and the high-frequency termination cadence Group-IB documented. Rationale: Targets ClickLock's exact victim-app set and the sub-second repeat cadence (200–210ms) Group-IB documented; a >20-kill-per-5-min burst against these GUI apps is not legitimate user behaviour. Threshold/temporal so no Sigma emitted.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1056.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A power user or script restarting the Dock/Finder once or twice to fix a hung UI
  • Login-hook or MDM script that killalls Dock/Finder to apply preferences
  • QA automation cycling apps rapidly on a test macOS host
  • Crash-recovery tooling relaunching frozen system apps
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and Parent !has "jamf" and Parent !has "munki"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the kill burst comes from a single non-system parent and coincides with an osascript password dialog on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Instruct the user to force-shutdown (hold power) and boot Safe Mode per Group-IB guidance; isolate the host in EDR. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate LaunchAgents in ~/Library/LaunchAgents for com.authirity/com.chromer plists and check for crontab/shell-profile persistence (GSocket).

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| order by KillCount desc

ClickLock LaunchAgent persistence (com.authirity.plist / com.chromer.plist) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the two named LaunchAgent property lists ClickLock drops to survive logout and relaunch its password-coercion modules at next login. Article-specific because both plist filenames are exact IOCs from Group-IB's report. Rationale: Both plist names (com.authirity.plist, com.chromer.plist) are exact filename IOCs from Group-IB; a FileCreated on either is unambiguous ClickLock persistence with near-zero benign overlap.
ATT&CKT1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely unlikely — these are unique malware-authored bundle IDs; only a security tool restoring a quarantined sample or an analyst reproducing the sample would create them
  • Backup/restore software rehydrating a previously infected user profile
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the plist's ProgramArguments to confirm it points at a ClickLock module path; note the writing process. Step 2 (contain): Unload with launchctl, delete both plists, isolate the host, and reset the user's login password. Step 3 (hunt): Check crontab and shell rc files (.zshrc/.bash_profile) for the GSocket backdoor, and sweep the fleet for these two filenames.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("com.authirity.plist","com.chromer.plist")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("com.authirity.plist","com.chromer.plist")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

ClickLock exfiltration/C2 to Telegram Bot API and GSocket relay from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts ClickLock's data theft and backdoor channels: ZIP-packaged stealer output uploaded via the Telegram Bot API and the GSocket reverse-shell relay, both initiated by shell/script binaries rather than a browser or the Telegram app. Article-specific because Group-IB names Telegram Bot API exfil and GSocket relay, and the campaign's compromised domains are included. Rationale: Combines the campaign's named channels (Telegram Bot API exfil, GSocket relay, gsnc.eu) with the compromised hosting domains, gated on shell/script initiators to strip legit browser/app Telegram traffic. api.telegram.org is dual-use, hence Medium confidence and the process gate.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DevOps notification script legitimately posting to api.telegram.org via curl
  • The official Telegram desktop app resolving api.telegram.org (excluded by initiator filter)
  • A sysadmin using GSocket/gs-netcat for legitimate remote support
  • Security scanner resolving the compromised domains during triage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".zip","sendDocument","sendMessage","bot") or RemoteUrl has "gsnc.eu"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For Telegram hits, dump InitiatingProcessCommandLine — look for a bot token/chat_id and a ZIP path (stealer archive); for gsnc.eu confirm the initiator is gs-netcat/gsocket. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, block all five domains, and revoke credentials that may have been in the archive (browser logins, wallet material, FileZilla creds). Step 3 (hunt): Trace back to the osascript password prompt, the kill-loop, and LaunchAgent/crontab persistence; sweep fleet for the same DNS queries.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.telegram.org","gsnc.eu","panalobet.ph","store.grafsynergy.com","cottonbox.co.il")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking","Brave Browser","Microsoft Edge","Telegram","Arc")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("curl","bash","sh","zsh","python","osascript","nohup","gs-netcat","gsocket")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery in~ ("api.telegram.org","gsnc.eu","panalobet.ph","store.grafsynergy.com","cottonbox.co.il")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3ce0504ba65f8d56f83d7fef45faeaeb31e4e5aa9b872b56610b5f2558231caa", "d9617710d4ed8e9b87f6fee0b7014c4101effba0", "b67aa4f598c0ea625a7409ea7884e10a7bc9c3ff", "8dda05168ea8610a2449419a47517bc32823d6ec", "0a1fb016bd10bac5455175c79aa4511e5ff1a330", "2fc970e25570532f9cbe33b7ebfe1f0383a7341a") or SHA1 in~ ("3ce0504ba65f8d56f83d7fef45faeaeb31e4e5aa9b872b56610b5f2558231caa", "d9617710d4ed8e9b87f6fee0b7014c4101effba0", "b67aa4f598c0ea625a7409ea7884e10a7bc9c3ff", "8dda05168ea8610a2449419a47517bc32823d6ec", "0a1fb016bd10bac5455175c79aa4511e5ff1a330", "2fc970e25570532f9cbe33b7ebfe1f0383a7341a") or MD5 in~ ("3ce0504ba65f8d56f83d7fef45faeaeb31e4e5aa9b872b56610b5f2558231caa", "d9617710d4ed8e9b87f6fee0b7014c4101effba0", "b67aa4f598c0ea625a7409ea7884e10a7bc9c3ff", "8dda05168ea8610a2449419a47517bc32823d6ec", "0a1fb016bd10bac5455175c79aa4511e5ff1a330", "2fc970e25570532f9cbe33b7ebfe1f0383a7341a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3ce0504ba65f8d56f83d7fef45faeaeb31e4e5aa9b872b56610b5f2558231caa", "d9617710d4ed8e9b87f6fee0b7014c4101effba0", "b67aa4f598c0ea625a7409ea7884e10a7bc9c3ff", "8dda05168ea8610a2449419a47517bc32823d6ec", "0a1fb016bd10bac5455175c79aa4511e5ff1a330", "2fc970e25570532f9cbe33b7ebfe1f0383a7341a") or SHA1 in~ ("3ce0504ba65f8d56f83d7fef45faeaeb31e4e5aa9b872b56610b5f2558231caa", "d9617710d4ed8e9b87f6fee0b7014c4101effba0", "b67aa4f598c0ea625a7409ea7884e10a7bc9c3ff", "8dda05168ea8610a2449419a47517bc32823d6ec", "0a1fb016bd10bac5455175c79aa4511e5ff1a330", "2fc970e25570532f9cbe33b7ebfe1f0383a7341a") or MD5 in~ ("3ce0504ba65f8d56f83d7fef45faeaeb31e4e5aa9b872b56610b5f2558231caa", "d9617710d4ed8e9b87f6fee0b7014c4101effba0", "b67aa4f598c0ea625a7409ea7884e10a7bc9c3ff", "8dda05168ea8610a2449419a47517bc32823d6ec", "0a1fb016bd10bac5455175c79aa4511e5ff1a330", "2fc970e25570532f9cbe33b7ebfe1f0383a7341a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3ce0504ba65f8d56f83d7fef45faeaeb31e4e5aa9b872b56610b5f2558231caa", "d9617710d4ed8e9b87f6fee0b7014c4101effba0", "b67aa4f598c0ea625a7409ea7884e10a7bc9c3ff", "8dda05168ea8610a2449419a47517bc32823d6ec", "0a1fb016bd10bac5455175c79aa4511e5ff1a330", "2fc970e25570532f9cbe33b7ebfe1f0383a7341a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Pheditor default-credential auth and terminal action against pheditor.php
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Pheditor terminal RCE: web-server/PHP process spawning an interactive shell
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Pheditor webshell drop: PHP/web-server process writing executable PHP files · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-55579: Pheditor: Hardcoded default password 'admin' w
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Pheditor terminal RCE: web-server/PHP process spawning an interactive shell AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-authentication terminal feature of Pheditor (CVE-2026-55579) being abused for command execution: a PHP/web-server process spawning /bin/sh, bash, dash etc. A web server spawning an interactive shell is the execution signature of the built-in terminal RCE reached via the hardcoded 'admin' default password. Rationale: PHP/web-server parent spawning an interactive shell is the direct execution artifact of Pheditor's built-in terminal (the article's 'terminal RCE'); web daemons almost never legitimately spawn shells, so the parent->child pair is high-fidelity. Anchored on the PHP binaries the app runs under, with an optional pheditor-in-cmdline enrichment for `php -S` deployments. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://github.com/pheditor/pheditor
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP applications that shell out via exec()/shell_exec()/proc_open() (e.g. ImageMagick wrappers, git-web hooks, backup cron triggers)
  • Web-based deployment/admin panels (Composer, artisan, wp-cli) that legitimately invoke the shell
  • Monitoring agents or health checks running as the web user that call /bin/sh
  • Container entrypoints where php-fpm launches a shell wrapper at startup
  • Developer/staging boxes where the app is intentionally allowed to run shell commands
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs ","gitolite","wp-cli","artisan","composer","healthcheck"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and the parent command line/folder path; confirm the shell was spawned by an internet-facing web daemon and inspect the command run (id/whoami/curl/wget indicate hands-on-keyboard). Check the source IP that hit the host at that time. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the web-server worker and shell process, and rotate any credentials readable by the web user; block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter. 3) Hunt: search the same host for new .php/.phar files written by the web user, for outbound connections from the shell (reverse shell / tool download), and for repeated POSTs to pheditor.php from the same IP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","php7.4","php8.1","php8.2","php8.3","httpd","apache2","nginx","caddy")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh")
| extend PheditorContext = InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "pheditor"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, PheditorContext, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","caddy")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh")
| extend PheditorContext = ParentProcessCommandLine has "pheditor"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, PheditorContext
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pheditor default-credential auth and terminal action against pheditor.php AIDelivery Low
Hunts inbound HTTP traffic to the Pheditor endpoint (pheditor.php) — POST logins and requests carrying action=terminal — which is how an attacker uses the hardcoded 'admin' default password (CVE-2026-55579) to reach the file-editor, upload and terminal features. Surfaces who is hitting a vulnerable, internet-exposed Pheditor instance. Rationale: The endpoint name pheditor.php, the login parameter pheditor_password=admin and the action=terminal parameter are verbatim article strings; access logs cannot see the POST body in most cases, so this is a hunting pivot to inventory who is reaching an exposed Pheditor and correlate with the host-side execution UC. WAFs that capture request bodies can match the literal default-password submission. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrators logging into and using their own Pheditor instance
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing for pheditor.php
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan/Censys/GreyNoise) fingerprinting the path
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors polling the login page
  • Security researchers or red team validating the advisory
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IPs hitting pheditor.php, whether the instance is internet-facing, and whether any request carried action=terminal or a successful (200) login; enrich source IPs against threat intel and geo. 2) Contain: if the instance is exposed with default creds, take it offline or firewall it, change the password, and verify no forced-change bypass; block hostile source IPs. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host-side execution UC (web server spawning shell) and webshell-write UC for the same host/time window to confirm whether reconnaissance became compromise.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "pheditor.php"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST" or RequestURL has "action=terminal" or RequestContext has_any ("pheditor_password=admin","action=terminal")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, DeviceCustomString1, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pheditor webshell drop: PHP/web-server process writing executable PHP files AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Pheditor file-upload/file-write feature (reached via the CVE-2026-55579 default password) being used to plant webshells or modify application code: a PHP/web-server process writing .php/.phar/.phtml files. Web servers rarely legitimately write new executable PHP, making this a strong persistence signal. Rationale: The article states the attacker can 'write/delete files, upload webshells, modify application code' via Pheditor's authenticated features; a web daemon writing new executable PHP into a webroot is the concrete on-disk artifact of that abuse and is rare in benign operation. Extensions and web-directory paths are the high-fidelity anchors. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate application deployments or auto-updates (Composer, CI/CD, WordPress/plugin updaters) writing PHP as the web user
  • PHP OPcache or template engines (Twig/Blade/Smarty) compiling cached .php files into cache dirs
  • Backup/restore tooling replacing application PHP files
  • Developers editing code in-place on a staging server
  • Pheditor being used legitimately by an authorized admin to edit or upload PHP
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "/cache/" and FolderPath !has "/tmp/" and FolderPath !has "/storage/framework/" and FolderPath !has "/var/cache/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file (FolderPath + SHA256) and inspect for webshell indicators (eval/base64_decode/system/assert/preg_replace-e, single-file obfuscation); check whether the writing process command line references pheditor and whether the file lives in a web-accessible path. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove confirmed webshell, isolate the host, and rotate secrets accessible to the web user; block the associated source IP. 3) Hunt: look for subsequent GET/POST requests to the newly written file, for the web server spawning shells (execution UC), and for the same file hash across other hosts.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","php7.4","php8.1","php8.2","php8.3","httpd","apache2","nginx","caddy")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua with double-slash path traversal to secrets (CVE-2026-53713) AIExploitation High
Hunts EnvoyExtensionPolicy create/update whose inline Lua contains the exact double-slash bypass paths (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) that defeat the is_critical_path check in security.lua. This is the concrete exploit signature for arbitrary file read from the Envoy Gateway controller pod during Strict validation. Rationale: Uses the exact double-slash payload paths named in the advisory (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) scoped to the envoyextensionpolicies resource — legitimate Lua policies never reference these. Cross-checked GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f and the related GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/CVE-2026-22771/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212 T1083
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team submitting a sanctioned validation/PoC policy to confirm patch status
  • Automated CVE-scanner or admission-controller test harness replaying the exploit manifest
  • A Lua policy that legitimately references /certs/ (single slash) mis-typed with a double slash by an operator
  • Backup/GitOps replay re-applying an old exploit manifest already stored in the repo
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !in ("system:serviceaccount:security-tools:cve-scanner") and UserAgent !has "validation-harness"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full requestObject for the flagged EnvoyExtensionPolicy and identify the submitting user/SA, source IP and userAgent; confirm the Lua references the double-slash sensitive paths. 2) Contain: delete the policy, rotate the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount token and any TLS keys reachable from the controller pod, and revoke the submitter's RBAC to create EnvoyExtensionPolicy. 3) Hunt: check the resource status/response for leaked token or file contents (see companion UC), and review kube audit for the envoy-gateway SA being used from unexpected sources afterward.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("//etc/passwd","//var/run/secrets","//proc/self/environ","//certs/")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), SrcIPs = tostring(User.extra)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" "objectRef.resource"="envoyextensionpolicies" (verb="create" OR verb="update" OR verb="patch")
| search requestObject="*//etc/passwd*" OR requestObject="*//var/run/secrets*" OR requestObject="*//proc/self/environ*" OR requestObject="*//certs/*"

Leaked SA token / file contents in EnvoyExtensionPolicy status (CVE-2026-53713 disclosure) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual secret disclosure: an envoyextensionpolicies audit record whose responseObject/status contains a JWT (service-account token), /etc/passwd content, or a PEM private key returned by the failed Strict validation. This confirms exploitation succeeded rather than just being attempted. Rationale: The related advisory confirms the SA token is 'returned in an error which will be displayed in the resource status'; eyJhbGciOi is the constant base64 prefix of a JWT header and root:x:0:0 is the invariant first line of /etc/passwd — both are high-fidelity content markers requiring RequestResponse-level audit. Cross-checked GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A policy legitimately referencing a JWT sample string in a comment (rare)
  • Audit policy not set to RequestResponse level so responseObject is empty (false negative, not FP)
  • Security testing that intentionally reproduces the disclosure in a lab cluster
  • A PEM string embedded in an unrelated but co-located config field captured in the same response
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the leaked material from responseObject — decode the JWT to identify which ServiceAccount was disclosed and its namespace/audience. 2) Contain: immediately rotate/delete that ServiceAccount token (delete the SA's token secret / bounce the pod to force projection refresh) and rotate any disclosed TLS private keys; treat the token as compromised. 3) Hunt: search kube audit for that SA's token being replayed (new sourceIPs, verbs it does not normally perform) and pivot to the companion token-reuse UC.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend RespStr = tostring(ResponseObject), StatusStr = tostring(ResponseStatus)
| where RespStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0","BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY","BEGIN PRIVATE KEY","serviceaccount/token") or StatusStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, ResponseStatus, RespStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua invoking os/io/debug file primitives AIExploitation Medium
Broader hunt for EnvoyExtensionPolicy manifests whose inline Lua calls filesystem/OS primitives (io.open, io.popen, os.getenv, os.execute, os.remove, debug.getinfo) — the building blocks any variant of this exploit needs to read the controller pod's files, catching payloads that use paths other than the four named in the advisory. Rationale: Reading a file from Lua requires io/os primitives; legitimate Envoy request-processing Lua manipulates headers/bodies and rarely touches io.open/os.execute, so their presence in a submitted policy is a strong pre-execution signal even when the payload uses a novel path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate advanced Lua filter that reads a mounted config file via io.open
  • os.getenv used to read a benign env var for routing logic
  • Developer testing a Lua snippet copied from a tutorial that includes os.time/os.date near os.execute
  • Vendor-provided policy template that legitimately uses debug for logging
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Lua body from requestObject and determine whether the io/os call targets sensitive paths or is benign routing logic. 2) Contain: if malicious, delete the policy and rotate controller credentials; if the cluster runs a vulnerable version, prioritise upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1. 3) Hunt: pivot to the double-slash and status-disclosure UCs for the same policy name and submitter.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("io.open","io.popen","os.getenv","os.execute","os.remove","debug.getinfo")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anomalous EnvoyExtensionPolicy submitter / suspicious policy name AIDelivery Medium
Profiles who creates EnvoyExtensionPolicy resources to surface rare submitters, and flags policy names containing exploit markers (poc, test, bypass, exploit, passwd). Because the exploit requires an attacker to create/patch the policy via the K8s API, unusual submitters are a leading indicator. Rationale: EnvoyExtensionPolicy objects are normally authored by a small, stable set of platform/GitOps identities; the summarize-by-submitter surfaces rare creators without a hard-coded allowlist, and the name markers catch dropped PoC manifests. Grouping/rarity is evaluated at rule level for Datadog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux SA) creating policies — high count, benign
  • A developer genuinely naming a policy 'canary-test' or 'lua-test'
  • First-time onboarding of a new platform engineer who legitimately creates a policy
  • CI pipeline SA applying policies from a new namespace
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for any rare submitter or exploit-marker name, retrieve the policy body and check for Lua io/os calls or double-slash paths. 2) Contain: if the submitter is unexpected, revoke their create/patch RBAC on envoyextensionpolicies and delete the policy. 3) Hunt: correlate the submitter identity across other CRDs and namespaces for further unauthorized changes.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), PolicyName = tostring(ObjectRef.name)
| extend SuspiciousName = PolicyName has_any ("poc","test","bypass","exploit","passwd")
| summarize Count=count(), Policies=make_set(PolicyName, 25), AnySuspicious=max(tolong(SuspiciousName)), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SubmitUser, UserAgent
| order by Count asc

Vulnerable Envoy Gateway version exposed to CVE-2026-53713 AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory hunt that flags hosts/images running an Envoy Gateway version affected by CVE-2026-53713 (>=1.8.0-rc.0 <1.8.1, or <1.7.4) so the exploitable surface is remediated to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 before an attacker submits a malicious EnvoyExtensionPolicy. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the affected/fixed version ranges from the advisory (fixed >=1.7.4 and >=1.8.1). This is the only pivot expressible on Defender/Sentinel native telemetry since the attack itself lives in K8s audit logs; relies on container/software vuln assessment picking up the envoyproxy/gateway package. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A patched version mis-fingerprinted by TVM as vulnerable (stale scan)
  • An image tag pinned to a fixed digest but labelled with an old version string
  • Non-production/lab Envoy Gateway flagged alongside prod
  • TVM not yet ingesting the CVE definition (false negative, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.7.4 or in 1.8.0-rc.0..1.8.1 and that the instance accepts EnvoyExtensionPolicy submissions. 2) Contain: restrict RBAC so only trusted identities can create/patch EnvoyExtensionPolicy, and apply the Lua-docs Warning-section workarounds until patched. 3) Hunt: upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 and retro-scan kube audit for prior exploit attempts against the affected cluster.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Envoy Gateway ServiceAccount token reuse for anomalous K8s API actions AIActions on Objectives Medium
Post-exploitation hunt: the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount (system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway) performing actions it never legitimately performs — creating/deleting pods, exec/attach into pods, reading kube-system secrets, or touching cluster RBAC — which indicates the disclosed token is being replayed against the API server. Rationale: The advisory states the disclosed token can be used to 'read sensitive information from the K8s API Server'; the envoy-gateway controller SA legitimately manages EnvoyProxy infra in its own namespace but never execs into pods, reads kube-system secrets, or edits cluster RBAC — so those verbs under that identity are strong reuse signals. SA name/namespace confirmed from Envoy Gateway deployment docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://gateway.envoyproxy.io/docs/tasks/operations/deployment-mode/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Envoy Gateway upgrade/migration job temporarily granting the SA broader RBAC
  • A future controller version that legitimately reads a secret in a shared namespace
  • Cluster admin impersonating the SA for troubleshooting (kubectl --as)
  • Backup tooling running under the same SA reading secrets broadly
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !startswith "envoy-gateway/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit compare sourceIPs and userAgent against the controller pod's normal client (in-cluster pod IP, controller userAgent); an external IP or kubectl/curl userAgent is high-confidence token theft. 2) Contain: rotate the envoy-gateway SA token immediately, cordon/quarantine any pods created by the SA, and review/revert RBAC changes. 3) Hunt: enumerate every action taken by the token since the disclosure event and check for new workloads, exfil connections, or additional credential reads.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), NS = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| where SubmitUser == "system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway"
| where (Verb in ("create","delete") and Resource in ("pods","pods/exec","pods/attach"))
     or (Resource == "secrets" and NS == "kube-system")
     or (Resource in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings","clusterroles"))
| project TimeGenerated, SubmitUser, Verb, Resource, NS, ObjName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ThreatsDay: Game Cheat Spyware, 24-Hour Ransomware, Chrome Sync Stalking + 12 More Stories

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputerCisco Talos
2026-07-16 24 use cases 13 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A lot of this week’s trouble starts with something that looks close enough. A familiar repo. A useful installer. A harmless sync setting. Then the handoff goes bad, the box starts talking to someone else, and the damage moves faster than the explanation. Old bugs are back, weak defaults are earning their keep, and some attack paths are so plain they barely feel like research. Here’s the mess.
