Starland RAT HWID-parameterized C2 / shellcode staging to UAT-11795 domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts host connections or DNS resolutions to UAT-11795's staging and C2 domains carrying the volume-serial HWID URL paths (/feed/, /alpha/) and raw shellcode paths (/starlandfox, /x32remka, /dopfile). Article-specific because it keys on the exact domain+path scheme Starland RAT uses to register victims and pull CastleStealer/Remcos shellcode. Rationale: Every listed domain is a confirmed UAT-11795 staging/C2 host; the /feed/, /alpha/ HWID paths and /starlandfox, /x32remka, /dopfile shellcode paths are unique campaign artifacts, so any resolution/connection is high-fidelity with near-zero legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1132.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox appliances deliberately resolving the IOC domains
  • A security researcher browsing the (possibly hijacked, still-legit) eorthopaedics.com storefront
  • Passive DNS collectors or SOAR playbooks pinging the domains for takedown verification
  • DNS sinkhole redirecting these domains, generating benign resolution logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the initiating process — python.exe/pythonw.exe or powershell.exe strongly indicates Starland RAT; note whether the URL carried a /feed/ or /alpha/ HWID path (victim already registered) or a shellcode path. 2. Contain: isolate the host, sinkhole/block all six domains, and capture memory before reboot (Starland decodes in memory). 3. Hunt: pivot on the volume-serial HWID string as the final URL path component across the estate, check for Polygon RPC fallback resolution (contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba), and Telegram beacons to bots 8384531459/7993597060.

Starland RAT Polygon smart-contract fallback C2 resolution (eth_call) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Starland RAT / mshta / PowerShell interpreters reaching Polygon (MATIC) public JSON-RPC endpoints, the backup C2-resolution channel that reads an XOR-encrypted fallback domain from smart contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba via eth_call. Article-specific because legitimate endpoints rarely query Polygon RPC from a scripting interpreter. Rationale: Article states Starland RAT resolves fallback C2 via eth_call to Polygon contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba; scoping Polygon RPC egress to scripting interpreters (not a browser or wallet app) isolates the RAT's blockchain-DGA behavior. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1568.002 T1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Crypto-tax or wallet-recovery tooling shelled from a script host
  • Blockchain data-analytics jobs on a workstation
  • Security researcher reproducing the eth_call to inspect the contract
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Roaming\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the initiating interpreter and its parent — a python.exe under a trojanized-installer tree hitting Polygon RPC is the RAT; a standalone dev script is likely benign. 2. Contain: isolate the host, block the Polygon RPC hosts for that endpoint, and capture memory to recover the decrypted fallback C2 domain. 3. Hunt: extract the resolved fallback domain and sweep the estate for it; correlate with contacts to the six primary domains and Telegram bot beacons; look for CastleStealer .NET stealer and Remcos artifacts.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) spawning shell — Spirals ASP.NET web shell initial access · [LLM] Remote Desktop enabled via fDenyTSConnections registry flip (Spirals persistence) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Spirals redundant remote access via revsocks / Chisel / Cloudflare tunnel · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Spirals ransomware payload masquerading as bitsadmin.exe outside System32 / via PsExec · [LLM] Spirals ransom note RECOVERY_SECTION.log dropped at drive root · [LLM] PowerShell mass-stop of backup/DB/virtualization services + Defender tampering (Spirals pre-encryption) · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change
Spirals ransomware payload masquerading as bitsadmin.exe outside System32 / via PsExec AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Spirals encryptor, which was named bitsadmin.exe to impersonate the legitimate BITS utility and deployed with PsExec running as SYSTEM. Flags any bitsadmin.exe executing from a non-System32/SysWOW64 path or spawned by PSEXESVC — the genuine utility never runs from those locations or under PsExec. Rationale: Article explicitly states the encryptor was named bitsadmin.exe to masquerade as the BITS utility and pushed via PsExec as SYSTEM; the genuine bitsadmin only lives in System32/SysWOW64 and never has PSEXESVC as parent, making location+parent a high-fidelity discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence • https://tugatech.com.pt/t87506-novo-ransomware-spirals-compromete-rede-empresarial-em-menos-de-24-horas
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party software bundling a renamed BITS helper in a vendor install directory
  • Sysadmin copying bitsadmin.exe to a scripts/tools folder for portable use
  • Security tooling running bitsadmin.exe from a quarantined/sandbox path
  • PsExec-based patch automation that legitimately relaunches system utilities
Suppression filter
| where not (SHA256 in (dynamic([])) ) // seed with your approved bitsadmin.exe hashes after first triage
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull SHA256 of the bitsadmin.exe hit and check reputation; a Rust-compiled binary with high entropy and no BITS version metadata confirms the impostor. Note the parent (PSEXESVC = SYSTEM push). Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host, kill the process tree, and block the hash org-wide via Defender/EDR custom indicator; disable the SYSTEM PsExec service account/source host. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for the same hash and for RECOVERY_SECTION.log; review PsExec source host for the operator's staging directory and lateral movement fan-out.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe"
| where (FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
     or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "PSEXESVC.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\bitsadmin.exe"
| where (not(NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" or NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64"))
     or ParentProcessName endswith @"\PSEXESVC.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Spirals Ransomware bitsadmin.exe Masquerade

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\bitsadmin.exe OR *\Bitsadmin.exe OR *\BITSADMIN.EXE) AND (@ParentImage:(*\PSEXESVC.exe OR *\psexesvc.exe OR *\PSEXESVC.EXE) OR NOT @Image:(C\:\Windows\System32\* OR C\:\Windows\SysWOW64\*))

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=bitsadmin.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT (match(process_path,"(?i)\\Windows\\System32\\") OR match(process_path,"(?i)\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\")) OR match(parent_process_name,"(?i)PSEXESVC\.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Spirals ransom note RECOVERY_SECTION.log dropped at drive root AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the Spirals ransom note file 'RECOVERY_SECTION.log', which the encryptor writes to C:\ after encrypting files. The filename is unique to this family, giving a near-zero-FP impact-stage indicator. Rationale: The article names the ransom note 'RECOVERY_SECTION.log' dropped on C:\; a fixed, family-unique filename is one of the highest-fidelity ransomware IOCs and requires no threshold logic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-spirals-ransomware-encrypts-victim-network-in-under-24-hours/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An analyst saving a copy of the extracted note for IR documentation on a live host
  • EDR/sandbox detonation of the sample writing the note in a test VM
  • Backup/restore tooling replaying an encrypted volume that already contains the note
  • A honeypot/canary deliberately seeded with the filename
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the note's parent folder — mass files with a new/blank extension and modified timestamps clustered around the write confirm active encryption. Identify InitiatingProcess (expect the fake bitsadmin.exe). Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from the network, suspend the encryptor process, and disable the compromised account; alert IR that encryption is in progress. Step 3 (hunt): Query all endpoints for the same filename to map blast radius, and correlate to PsExec pushes from the operator host to catch machines queued but not yet encrypted.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "RECOVERY_SECTION.log"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "RECOVERY_SECTION.log"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PowerShell mass-stop of backup/DB/virtualization services + Defender tampering (Spirals pre-encryption) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Spirals pre-encryption PowerShell payload that disabled Microsoft Defender, removed threat definitions, and stopped 23 backup, database, and virtualization services (Veeam, VMware, Hyper-V, SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL) to inhibit recovery. Fires when a shell command targets those product service names with a stop/disable verb, or performs Defender tampering. Rationale: Article specifies a single PowerShell payload that disabled Defender, removed definitions, and stopped 23 named backup/DB/virtualization services (Veeam, VMware, Hyper-V, SQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL); pairing those product service tokens with a stop verb, or Defender-tamper cmdlets, targets the exact pre-encryption behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence • https://tugatech.com.pt/t87506-novo-ransomware-spirals-compromete-rede-empresarial-em-menos-de-24-horas
ATT&CKT1489 T1562.001 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/SQL backup jobs stopping their own services during maintenance windows
  • VMware/Hyper-V host patching that cycles vmms/vmcompute
  • Sysadmin scripts disabling a DB service before an upgrade
  • EDR migration playbooks toggling Set-MpPreference during Defender offboarding
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","sqlservr.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether the shell stopped MULTIPLE distinct product services in one burst and whether Defender realtime protection was disabled — a legitimate maintenance job touches one product, not Veeam+VMware+SQL together. Check the initiating account and remote-session flag. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, re-enable Defender tamper protection, and disable the account; treat encryption as imminent. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the same account/host for WMI lateral movement and PsExec pushes, and hunt for RECOVERY_SECTION.log and the fake bitsadmin.exe fleet-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","net.exe","sc.exe")
| where (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Veeam","VMware","vmms","MSSQL","SQLSERVERAGENT","OracleService","postgresql","vmcompute","MSExchange")
         and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Stop-Service","net stop","sc stop","Set-Service"))
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","-RemoveDefinitions","Set-MpPreference","MpCmdRun.exe -RemoveDefinitions")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","net.exe","sc.exe")
| where (CommandLine has_any ("Veeam","VMware","vmms","MSSQL","SQLSERVERAGENT","OracleService","postgresql","vmcompute","MSExchange")
         and CommandLine has_any ("Stop-Service","net stop","sc stop","Set-Service"))
   or CommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","-RemoveDefinitions","Set-MpPreference")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|cmd|net|sc)\.exe$/i
| (regex("(?i)(Veeam|VMware|vmms|MSSQL|SQLSERVERAGENT|OracleService|postgresql|vmcompute)", field=CommandLine) AND regex("(?i)(Stop-Service|net stop|sc stop|Set-Service)", field=CommandLine)) OR regex("(?i)(DisableRealtimeMonitoring|-RemoveDefinitions|Set-MpPreference)", field=CommandLine)

Spirals redundant remote access via revsocks / Chisel / Cloudflare tunnel AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the redundant C2/tunneling tooling Spirals established — revsocks, Chisel, and Cloudflare tunnels (cloudflared) — by binary name or characteristic tunnel command-line arguments. Covers the operator's persistence of remote access separate from RDP. Rationale: Article names revsocks, Chisel, and Cloudflare tunnels as the redundant remote-access channels; corroborated by Symantec/TugaTech coverage. Binary names plus tunnel-specific args (trycloudflare.com, chisel's R:socks reverse-SOCKS, cloudflared 'tunnel run') target the exact tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.chisel
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately running cloudflared for a sanctioned Cloudflare Tunnel to internal apps
  • Red-team/pentest engagements using Chisel for authorized pivoting
  • IT using revsocks/Chisel for troubleshooting remote connectivity
  • cloudflared auto-update service restarting an approved named tunnel
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel run" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (dynamic(["--config"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine if the tunnel destination and binary are sanctioned — check whether cloudflared runs a named, ticketed tunnel vs an ephemeral trycloudflare.com URL, and whether Chisel/revsocks exist in any approved software inventory. Step 2 (contain): Kill the tunnel process, block the C2 domain/IP at egress, and isolate the host if paired with any Spirals indicator. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the tunnel process's network egress to identify the operator's external endpoint, and check the same host for the fake bitsadmin.exe, RDP enablement, and WMI lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has_any ("revsocks","chisel","cloudflared")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("trycloudflare.com","R:socks","tunnel run","--url http")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("revsocks","chisel","cloudflared")
     or CommandLine has_any ("trycloudflare.com","R:socks","tunnel run","--url http")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) spawning shell — Spirals ASP.NET web shell initial access AIInstallation High
Detects the Spirals initial-access vector: an ASP.NET web shell on a public IIS server causing w3wp.exe to spawn command shells and recon/LOLBin utilities. Scopes strictly to the IIS worker parent so it targets the web-shell foothold rather than generic script execution. Rationale: Article states initial access was via an ASP.NET web shell uploaded to a public IIS server; scoping to w3wp.exe (the IIS worker) spawning shells/recon LOLBins targets the exact web-shell foothold, and captures the follow-on discovery Spirals ran under that context. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/dissecting-a-warlock-attack.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately shelling out to run reports or batch jobs from application code
  • APM/monitoring agents invoked by the app pool identity
  • Deployment/CI tooling that runs powershell under the IIS app pool during release
  • Admin using an approved web-based management console that spawns cmd
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "powershell.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (dynamic(["-appPoolName","DeploymentAgent"])))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Review the child command line and the IIS site/app-pool involved; recon commands (whoami, nltest, net) or bitsadmin/certutil downloads under w3wp confirm web-shell abuse. Pull recent IIS logs (W3CIISLog) for the requesting IP and the suspicious .aspx URL. Step 2 (contain): Take the site offline or block the attacker IP, remove the web-shell .aspx, and isolate the server. Step 3 (hunt): Identify the dropped web-shell file via file-create events under the web root, and pivot from this host to RDP-enable registry changes, new local accounts, and WMI lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","reg.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","reg.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote Desktop enabled via fDenyTSConnections registry flip (Spirals persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Spirals persistence step of enabling RDP by setting HKLM Terminal Server 'fDenyTSConnections' to 0. Pairs naturally with the local-account creation the operator used to retain access on the compromised host. Rationale: Article states the operator enabled Remote Desktop for persistence; the canonical mechanism is flipping HKLM\...\Terminal Server\fDenyTSConnections to 0, a specific registry value+data pair that is a high-fidelity persistence indicator when done by an interactive/attacker process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin legitimately enabling RDP on a new server via Server Manager or GPO
  • MDM/Intune configuration baseline turning on RDP
  • Approved remote-support tooling enabling RDP during a maintenance window
  • Golden-image build process setting fDenyTSConnections=0
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("svchost.exe","mmc.exe","ServerManager.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and account — an interactive shell (cmd/powershell/reg.exe) or web-shell child flipping this value, rather than GPO/Server Manager, is suspicious. Check for a co-occurring new local account (Security 4720) on the same host. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorized, re-set fDenyTSConnections to 1, disable/remove the attacker-created local account, and restrict RDP at the firewall; isolate if other Spirals indicators are present. Step 3 (hunt): Look for inbound RemoteInteractive (LogonType 10) logons to the host after the change, and pivot to WMI lateral movement and the tunneling tools used for redundant access.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "fDenyTSConnections"
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryValue =~ "fDenyTSConnections"
| where RegistryValueData == "0" or RegistryValueData has "0x00000000"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Spirals Ransomware RDP Enable via fDenyTSConnections Registry Flip

#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate RegValueName=/fDenyTSConnections$/i RegStringValue=/^0/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, RegStringValue, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_value_name=fDenyTSConnections Registry.registry_value_data=0 by Registry.dest Registry.registry_key_name Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_value_name=fDenyTSConnections Registry.registry_value_data=0 by Registry.dest Registry.registry_key_name Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

Unpatched Shark Vacuum Flaw Could Let Attackers Control Other Vacuums Region-Wide

The Hacker News
2026-07-16 3 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

Pull the certificate off the flash of a Shark RV2320EDUS robot vacuum, and you can run root commands on other people's Shark vacuums across the same AWS region: watch the camera, drive the robot, read the map of the house, and take the Wi-Fi password in plaintext. A researcher publishing under the handle tokay0&nbsp;put the method online&nbsp;on Monday, having tested it only against vacuums he

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] AWS IoT client subscribing to reserved wildcard topic $aws/things/# (Shark vacuum serial harvest)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] AWS IoT policy created/updated granting reserved $aws/things/* topic without ThingName pinning
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Single AWS IoT principal writing shadows to multiple distinct device thing names (cross-device Exec_Command RCE)
AWS IoT client subscribing to reserved wildcard topic $aws/things/# (Shark vacuum serial harvest) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts a single MQTT principal/certificate subscribing to the reserved wildcard shadow topic $aws/things/# (or /+), the exact reconnaissance step tokay0 used against Shark's IoT broker to enumerate 1.5M device serial numbers. A correctly scoped device only ever subscribes to its own $aws/things/<thingName>/... topics, so a wildcard subscribe to the reserved things namespace is anomalous by definition. Rationale: Uses the article's exact recon string ($aws/things/# wildcard subscribe) — AWS's own IOT_POLICY_OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_CHECK docs confirm subscribing to the reserved things namespace is the abuse pattern, so a single principal doing it is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot-device-defender/latest/devguide/audit-chk-iot-policy-permissive.html • https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/iot/identify-misconfigured-iot-policies-using-aws-iot-device-defender/
ATT&CKT1580 T1078.001
Data sourcesAWS IoT Core logs
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backend fleet-management service intentionally provisioned with a broad subscribe policy (should be an allow-listed service principal, not a device cert)
  • IoT platform monitoring/observability tooling subscribing to reserved topics for diagnostics
  • AWS IoT Device Defender or a SIEM connector using a service certificate to mirror device shadows
  • Load/soak-test harnesses in a non-prod account exercising many things
Suppression filter
| where principalId!="<known-fleet-service-cert>"  -- maintain an allow-list of legitimate backend service certificate IDs
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the clientId/principalId/sourceIp from the hit and confirm whether the principal is a per-device certificate (attacker) or a known backend service cert (likely benign). Check the source IP geolocation/ASN against expected device fleet ranges. 2) Contain: if it is a device certificate, revoke/deactivate that certificate (UpdateCertificate INACTIVE) and detach its policy; the same cert cannot re-subscribe once revoked. 3) Hunt: from that principalId, pull all subsequent Publish/UpdateThingShadow events to enumerate which device shadows it touched, and correlate with the cross-device shadow-write UC.
# log group: AWSIotLogsV2
fields @timestamp, clientId, principalId, sourceIp, eventType, topicName
| filter eventType = "Subscribe"
| filter topicName like /^\$aws\/things\/[#+]/
| stats count(*) as subscribes, count_distinct(topicName) as topics by clientId, principalId, sourceIp
| sort subscribes desc
APPLICATION
index=aws sourcetype="aws:iot" eventType=Subscribe (topicName="$aws/things/#" OR topicName="$aws/things/+" OR topicName="$aws/things/*")
| stats count AS subscribes values(topicName) AS topics min(_time) AS firstSeen by clientId principalId sourceIp
| sort - subscribes
Single AWS IoT principal writing shadows to multiple distinct device thing names (cross-device Exec_Command RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts one MQTT certificate/principal publishing UpdateThingShadow to more than one distinct thing name — the cross-device shadow-write that delivers the Exec_Command field to appd's execute_command()/popen on victim Shark vacuums. A legitimately scoped device only ever writes its own shadow, so any principal addressing multiple thing names is the attack's execution step. Rationale: Directly targets the article's execution primitive (an attacker cert publishing shadow updates carrying Exec_Command to any device topic); the topicName carries the target thingName, so distinct-thing fan-out from one principal is a clean behavioural signature of cross-device control. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot-device-defender/latest/devguide/audit-chk-iot-policy-permissive.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1078.001
Data sourcesAWS IoT Core logs
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate fleet-orchestration backend that pushes shadow updates (jobs, OTA config) to many devices under one service principal — allow-list it
  • A gateway/hub device that proxies shadow state for several child devices it legitimately owns
  • Provisioning tooling bulk-initialising shadows during device onboarding
  • Migration scripts re-writing shadow documents during an account/region move
Suppression filter
| where principalId!="<known-fleet-orchestration-cert>"  -- allow-list legitimate multi-device backend certificate IDs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the principalId and list the distinct thingNames it wrote; if the principal is a per-device certificate but touched multiple thing names, treat as confirmed cross-device control. Inspect (if payload logging/republish rule exists) the shadow document for an Exec_Command field. 2) Contain: deactivate the offending certificate, then push a scoped policy version (CreatePolicyVersion + setAsDefault) pinning topics to ${iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName}; disconnect/quarantine affected thing names. 3) Hunt: for each victim thingName, review outbound NetworkConnectIP/Exec_Response traffic for reverse-shell callbacks and camera-stream egress; pivot on sourceIp across regions for additional certificates.
# log group: AWSIotLogsV2
fields @timestamp, clientId, principalId, sourceIp, eventType, topicName
| filter (eventType = "UpdateThingShadow" or eventType = "Publish")
| filter topicName like /^\$aws\/things\/.+\/shadow\/update$/
| parse topicName "$aws/things/*/shadow/update" as thingName
| stats count_distinct(thingName) as distinctThings, count(*) as writes by clientId, principalId, sourceIp
| filter distinctThings > 1
| sort distinctThings desc
APPLICATION
index=aws sourcetype="aws:iot" (eventType=UpdateThingShadow OR eventType=Publish) topicName="$aws/things/*/shadow/update"
| rex field=topicName "\$aws/things/(?<thingName>[^/]+)/shadow/update"
| stats dc(thingName) AS distinctThings count values(sourceIp) AS srcIps by clientId principalId
| where distinctThings > 1
| sort - distinctThings
AWS IoT policy created/updated granting reserved $aws/things/* topic without ThingName pinning AIWeaponization Medium
Detects CreatePolicy/CreatePolicyVersion CloudTrail events whose policyDocument grants publish/subscribe on the reserved topicfilter/$aws/things/* namespace without the ${iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName} constraint — the exact IOT_POLICY_OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_CHECK shape that made the Shark certificate a region-wide skeleton key. Surfaces the root-cause misconfiguration at provisioning time. Rationale: Encodes AWS's own critical audit finding (IOT_POLICY_OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_CHECK) as a real-time CloudTrail detection using the concrete policyDocument tell (reserved $aws/things/* topicfilter minus the ThingName pin) the article names as the root cause. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot-device-defender/latest/devguide/audit-chk-iot-policy-permissive.html • https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2022/12/aws-iot-device-defender-audit-identifies-potential-misconfiguration-iot-policies/
ATT&CKT1098 T1552.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backend/gateway service policy that intentionally needs broad shadow access (should be explicitly reviewed and allow-listed)
  • Infrastructure-as-code (Terraform/CDK) baseline that ships a permissive template later scoped down
  • Device Defender remediation tooling reissuing a corrected policy (contains ThingName pin — excluded by the filter)
  • Vendor sample/quick-start policy applied in a dev/test account
Suppression filter
| where userIdentity.arn!="<known-iac-provisioning-role-arn>" and requestParameters.policyName!="<approved-backend-service-policy>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the created policyDocument, confirm it grants iot:Subscribe/iot:Receive/iot:Publish on topicfilter/$aws/things/* or resource * with no ${iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName} constraint, and identify which certificates/thing groups it is attached to. 2) Contain: push a scoped replacement with CreatePolicyVersion + setAsDefault (per AWS remediation) so every certificate using the policy is immediately re-scoped; where feasible, reissue affected device certificates. 3) Hunt: run a Device Defender on-demand audit for IOT_POLICY_OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_CHECK across all regions, and review AWSIotLogsV2 for any principal that already exercised the broad grant (wildcard subscribe or cross-device shadow writes).
title: AWS IoT Policy Created With Overly Permissive Reserved Thing Topic
id: 2f9c4e17-6b3a-4d21-9a5e-7c1b0f8e3a44
status: experimental
description: Detects an AWS IoT policy created or versioned that grants access to the reserved $aws/things/* topicfilter without pinning to the connecting thing name, the misconfiguration behind the Shark vacuum region-wide RCE.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-shark-vacuum-flaw-could-let.html
  - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot-device-defender/latest/devguide/audit-chk-iot-policy-permissive.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1098
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: iot.amazonaws.com
    eventName:
      - CreatePolicy
      - CreatePolicyVersion
    requestParameters.policyDocument|contains: 'topicfilter/$aws/things/*'
  filter_scoped:
    requestParameters.policyDocument|contains: 'iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName'
  condition: selection and not filter_scoped
falsepositives:
  - Intentional broad backend/service policies (should be reviewed and allow-listed)
level: high
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(CreatePolicy OR CreatePolicyVersion) @requestParameters.policyDocument:*topicfilter/$aws/things/* -@requestParameters.policyDocument:*iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName*
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.policyName
| filter eventSource = "iot.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["CreatePolicy", "CreatePolicyVersion"]
      and requestParameters.policyDocument like /topicfilter\/\$aws\/things\/\*/
      and not (requestParameters.policyDocument like /iot:Connection\.Thing\.ThingName/)
| sort @timestamp desc
CLOUD
index=aws sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventSource="iot.amazonaws.com" (eventName=CreatePolicy OR eventName=CreatePolicyVersion) requestParameters.policyDocument="*topicfilter/$aws/things/*" NOT requestParameters.policyDocument="*iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName*"
| table _time eventName userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress requestParameters.policyName
| sort - _time

OpenAI’s GPT-Red Automates Prompt Injection Testing to Harden GPT-5.6 Sol

The Hacker News

Unpatched Zoom Workplace/VDI/Meeting SDK for Windows (CVE-2026-53412 account-takeover + privesc set) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Windows endpoints whose installed Zoom client is exposed to the July 2026 Zoom advisory CVEs (CVE-2026-53412 unauthenticated network account takeover, plus CVE-2026-53411/53410/53409 local privilege escalation / TOCTOU). This is an exposure-identification hunt driven off the exact CVE IDs from the advisory, not attack detection — none of these flaws were observed exploited in the wild, so the value is prioritising patch remediation of the critical 9.8 client-takeover bug. Rationale: Built entirely on the four concrete CVE IDs published in the Zoom advisory (CVE-2026-53412/53411/53410/53409) and the affected products (Zoom Workplace, VDI Client/Plugin, Meeting SDK, Rooms for Windows) — CVE-ID matching against a maintained vuln feed is zero-false-positive on the identifier itself, and the article states no exploit strings exist to hunt on, so exposure identification is the only high-fidelity option. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/zoom-warns-of-critical-account-takeover-vulnerability/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195454/security/zoom-fixes-cve-2026-53412-a-critical-account-takeover-bug.html • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-53412
ATT&CKT1203 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched but within the MDVM/scanner rescan lag window (up to 24h) so still reported vulnerable
  • Endpoint inside an approved maintenance window scheduled to receive the Zoom update within SLA — not a genuine gap
  • VDI plugin branch-version mismatch: a 6.5.x-branch host on 6.5.18 is fixed even though a naive version compare against 6.6.14 flags it
  • Kiosk/Zoom Rooms appliances managed outside the standard patch pipeline that a vendor handles on its own cadence
  • Third-party scanner mis-fingerprinting a non-Windows or SDK-embedded Zoom component that does not carry the vulnerable client code

Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache AIDelivery High
Hunts for the five backdoored @asyncapi package versions (@asyncapi/specs 6.11.2 & 6.11.2-alpha.1, generator 3.3.1, generator-components 0.7.1, generator-helpers 1.1.1) landing on developer/CI hosts via npm or Yarn dependency resolution. Article-specific because it pins the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft/Socket confirmed, not generic 'npm install' activity. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft published and Socket/StepSecurity independently confirmed; package name is always lowercase in the registry/cache so no casing enumeration needed, and version+name combined is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or IR teams intentionally downloading the malicious versions into a sandbox for analysis
  • An internal mirror/Artifactory that cached the bad versions during the exposure window and is now being audited
  • Developers who pinned 6.11.2 in a lockfile and re-ran install against a still-poisoned private proxy
  • Yarn/npm cache directories restored from an old backup image containing the version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","yarn.exe","npm-cli.js") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("malware-analysis","sandbox","detonate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path is a real install target (node_modules, .yarn/cache, npm _cacache) and not a knowingly-collected sample; capture the host, user, and whether it's a dev box or CI runner. 2) Contain: isolate the host, purge npm & Yarn caches, remove all five affected versions, and pin @asyncapi/specs to a known-good release; block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 at egress. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to a detached node child writing sync.js under the NodeJS masquerade dir and any outbound IPFS fetch; rotate every credential reachable from that environment (npm tokens, GitHub CLI, AWS, SSH keys).

Second-stage sync.js dropped under OS 'NodeJS' masquerade directory AIInstallation High
Detects the import-time loader writing its IPFS-fetched second stage as sync.js into the OS-specific NodeJS masquerade folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS, ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS, ~/.config/NodeJS). Article-specific: the fixed filename sync.js plus the fake NodeJS directory is a unique fingerprint of this campaign, not generic file drops. Rationale: Uses the verbatim FILE_NAME='sync.js' constant and the getTargetDirectory() 'NodeJS' masquerade paths from the article's code block 2 — the combination is unique to this loader and confirmed by Microsoft's own Query 1. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool that genuinely names its data dir 'NodeJS' and writes a sync.js sync script
  • Developer scaffolding/boilerplate that creates a sync.js worker under an app-support folder
  • A backup/restore of a previously-infected profile re-materializing sync.js
  • Security tooling replaying the sample into a NodeJS folder during analysis
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "npm" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "yarn"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash sync.js and check its parent process — a node.exe/node child with detached/hidden flags confirms; benign scripts have a real signed parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node process tree, delete sync.js, and block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 plus ipfs.io retrieval at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot to which @asyncapi version installed on the host, look for outbound IPFS CID fetches (Qmet4… / QmQobZSp…), and rotate all credentials reachable from the environment given Miasma's credential-harvest module.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where FolderPath has "NodeJS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "NodeJS"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detached hidden node.exe executing sync.js from NodeJS masquerade path AIInstallation High
Detects the import-time payload's execution stage: a node process launching the dropped sync.js out of the NodeJS masquerade directory, matching the spawn('node',[payloadPath],{detached,stdio:ignore,windowsHide}) pattern. Article-specific via the sync.js + NodeJS command-line pairing (mirrors Microsoft's published hunting Query 1). Rationale: Combines the verbatim FILE_NAME 'sync.js' and 'NodeJS' masquerade path from code block 2 with a node interpreter parent — the same signal Microsoft ships as their behavioral coverage for the detached Node.js spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Electron/CLI tooling that stores helper scripts under an app-support NodeJS folder
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a sandbox VM
  • A monorepo build task named sync.js executed with a NodeJS-prefixed cwd
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jest","webpack","vite","--build") and DeviceName has "build")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full command line and grandparent — a build/import node.exe (from npm/yarn) spawning this detached child confirms the chain; note the SHA256 of sync.js. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the detached node tree, remove sync.js, and block the C2 IP/ports and IPFS egress. 3) Hunt: correlate to the affected @asyncapi version on the host and any outbound connection to 85.137.53.71 or ipfs.io CIDs within minutes; force credential rotation for npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH accessible from that host.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName has "node"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "sync.js"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "NodeJS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Outbound C2 to Miasma controller 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Miasma runtime's command-and-control beaconing to the hardcoded controller 85.137.53.71 over its three fixed ports. Article-specific: a single named IP plus the exact non-standard port trio Microsoft told orgs to block — near-zero ambiguity. Rationale: Single hardcoded controller IP plus the exact port trio (8080/8081/8091) that Microsoft explicitly recommended blocking — a definitive C2 indicator with essentially no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-asyncapi-npm-supply-chain-attack-delivers-multi-stage-miasma-botnet-via-compromised-github-act • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/
ATT&CKT1571 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/IR analyst deliberately connecting to the C2 for characterization from a sanctioned sandbox
  • A honeypot or deception host configured to beacon to known-bad IPs
  • Vulnerability scanner probing the IP as part of an external asset sweep
  • Reuse of 85.137.53.71 by an unrelated benign service after takedown (verify recency)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — node.exe/sync.js confirms Miasma; capture host, user, and beacon cadence. 2) Contain: isolate host, block 85.137.53.71 on 8080/8081/8091 at perimeter and host firewall, and kill the responsible process tree. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same IP/ports and for the decentralized fallback channels (Nostr, Ethereum, BitTorrent DHT, libp2p, IPFS); enumerate which imported @asyncapi and rotate every reachable credential.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71"
| where RemotePort in (8080, 8081, 8091)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
| where DstPortNumber in (8080, 8081, 8091)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DstDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS gateway (specific CIDs) AIDelivery High
Detects the child loader fetching sync.js from IPFS via ipfs.io, keyed on the two campaign CIDs (Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf for specs, QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9 for the generator family) or any node process hitting the ipfs.io gateway. Article-specific via the exact IPFS content identifiers. Rationale: Uses the two verbatim IPFS CIDs from the article's Table 2 and the ipfs.io gateway constant from code block 2; a node interpreter fetching from ipfs.io is itself anomalous in most enterprises and the CID match is definitive. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1105 T1102
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Web3/blockchain developer legitimately pinning or fetching content from ipfs.io via a Node app
  • CI jobs that pull assets from public IPFS gateways
  • Browser-based IPFS usage co-resident on a dev workstation (not node-initiated)
  • Analyst reproducing the fetch of the campaign CIDs in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("web3","blockchain") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ipfs-http-client")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node.exe and whether the URL contains a campaign CID (definitive) vs generic ipfs.io (assess node context). 2) Contain: isolate host, block ipfs.io egress for server/build subnets, kill the node process, and remove any sync.js written afterward. 3) Hunt: correlate the fetch time to a preceding @asyncapi install and a following connection to 85.137.53.71; check other hosts for the same CIDs and rotate credentials exposed to the environment.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has_any ("Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"))
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName has "node" and RemoteUrl contains "ipfs.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9")
    or Url has "ipfs.io/ipfs/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
